content.text: Falanaras reached Silvermoon’s eastern gate before dawn, summoned in full armor and carrying orders that named only a southern deployment.

The departure yard was already awake. Quartermasters moved between provision carts with slate boards and bad tempers. Armorers checked shield rims beneath mage-light. A stablehand swore at a hawkstrider that had learned to bite anyone wearing a red sash.

Nothing in the preparations suggested ceremony. The wagons carried field dressings, spare bowstrings, warding rods, and grain sealed against wet weather. Officers spoke in the clipped tones used when the destination had been withheld from most of the column and the people who knew it disliked the answer.

The Horde banner hung beside the phoenix above Silvermoon’s eastern gate. Its warding held. An obscenity crossed the lower stone in hurried black paint, shorter and less inventive than the last one. Citizens passed beneath the foreign colors on their way to the mana stalls, arguing over prices without looking up.

Falanaras crossed beneath both standards in black plate edged with crimson. The breastplate Edric had broken was gone. Its replacement carried a reinforced seam over the ribs and a shallow dent near the heart from another field, another weapon, another report already filed. He no longer noticed which soldiers looked first at the red-gold Light resting along his sword belt and which looked at his green eyes.
He noticed when they failed to make room.

The departure yard held more Blood Knights than it had on the march to Hillsbrad. Two files stood behind Theron with black shields planted against the paving. Their armor varied in age and finish; the order had grown faster than Silvermoon’s smiths could make uniform plate. The crimson edging and governed radiance made them one body despite the differences.

Farstriders gathered beneath Lethira’s inspection. She had acquired a narrow scar across her left hand and an orcish knife at her belt. She refused to explain either to anyone who had not been present, which meant she had explained both at length to everyone who had.
“Your third file is crooked,” she told Theron.
Theron looked without turning his head. “Your second ranger is wearing two different boots.”
“One of them fits.”
“Then we are equally prepared.”
Lethira’s mouth twitched. Theron had already turned to the quartermaster’s slate, the matter of mismatched boots settled to his satisfaction.
Liadrin entered the yard with four senior knights and a sealed order beneath her arm. Conversation ended by degrees as each file saw her.
“The Portal has been open long enough for fools to mistake endurance for containment,” she said. “That error has ended.”

A magister unfolded a map on the quartermaster’s table. Black markers occupied the Blasted Lands around the standing gateway. Smaller marks spread east along the roads and north beyond the region’s barren ridges. Several had been crossed out. More remained.

“Demonic bands have struck caravans in the Swamp of Sorrows, farms beyond the mountain roads, and settlements that believed the Blasted Lands were distance enough,” Liadrin continued. “The Alliance has begun moving soldiers toward the Portal. The Horde has done the same. Neither faction intends to surrender the crossing to the other. Both understand what happens if the Legion keeps it.”
“Do they understand together?” Lethira asked.
“No,” Liadrin said. “They understand in parallel.”
Several rangers smiled. No one mistook the answer for reassurance.

Liadrin placed one gauntleted hand on the map where the gateway stood. Falanaras felt M’uru answer her through the bond beneath his breastbone. The naaru’s suffering had changed neither pitch nor meaning during the year. Falanaras had changed around it. He could march, heal, kill, eat, sleep, and wake with that distant anguish inside every act of power. Familiarity had made the burden easier to carry and harder to excuse.

“The Blood Knights will go as Silvermoon’s first heavy contingent,” Liadrin said. “Rangers will scout the road and the far-side ground. Magisters will support the Portal works if any remain recoverable. You will serve within Gorath Stonebinder’s column until the threshold is secured. Beyond it, command may change with the field.”

The name produced no unease among the files. A year earlier, serving under an orc had required a council decision and a public test. Now quartermasters asked only how much grain his column carried and whether his scouts knew the road.
Liadrin looked directly at Falanaras. “You have crossed before.”
“When the road belonged to the prince.”
“It belongs to no one now. Help make that temporary.”
Falanaras bowed. “Discipline. Duty. Honor. Remembrance.”
The response came from the knights behind him, many voices carrying the same four burdens.

They reached the Horde mustering ground through a chain of transit circles that left the sin’dorei magisters pale and irritable. The last opened beneath wet trees in the Swamp of Sorrows. Humid air entered Falanaras’s armor before he cleared the runes. The camp beyond smelled of mud, boiled grain, troll incense, wet hides, and the alchemical preservatives used to keep Forsaken supplies from becoming more dead than intended.

Gorath waited beside a row of loaded wagons. He had added two more carved stones to his belt since Hillsbrad. The left shoulder Falanaras had once injured moved without stiffness. A pale line crossed one tusk where some later weapon had failed to remove it.
“Silvermoon sent more of you,” he said.
“You kept returning the ones we sent,” Falanaras replied.

Gorath examined him for mockery, found only enough to acknowledge, and struck one fist against Falanaras’s shoulder plate. It was an orc greeting he had begun using after a road neither of them mentioned. Falanaras returned it against the shaman’s leather guard.

Jazreth Shadowtide sat beneath the wagon awning with rain passing through the edge of the darkness around him. He had painted a thin white line across his nose and replaced several bone charms with demon teeth. “Elf finally arrives. I was starting to enjoy de quiet.”
“You complained through the entire last watch we shared.”
“Quiet makes room for important complaints.”

Mavren Coldwake emerged from behind the wagons carrying a crate under his left arm. The severed limb from Hillsbrad had been reattached, though the wrist turned a fraction too far when he set the crate down. He had compensated by fastening his shield grip at an angle.
“Your healers continue to insist the arm is functional,” he said to Theron. “I continue to define function more strictly.”
Theron inspected the wrist. “You use it to complain.”
“Then perhaps they exceeded expectation.”

Tahu Windtotem stood among the draft beasts, calming a wolf whose hackles had risen at the Blood Knights’ approach. The tauren’s horns carried fresh red cord and one dark burn near the tip. He rested his broad hand between the wolf’s ears until the animal stopped watching the stolen Light.
“The wound in your radiance remains,” Tahu said when Falanaras reached him.
“Yes.”

Tahu nodded. He no longer asked whether Falanaras intended to mend it. Acceptance from the tauren had never meant approval. It meant he trusted Falanaras to answer the same question truthfully each time.

The column marched west before noon. Orc infantry led the supply wagons. Darkspear scouts moved through the wet ground on either flank. Tauren walked where the road widened, carrying loads that had required teams of smaller soldiers. Forsaken outriders disappeared into mist and returned without breath or warning. The blood elf files occupied the center beneath phoenix standards that no longer looked misplaced among the Horde’s red banners.

Trust showed itself in assignment. Gorath put Theron’s shield file beside the ammunition wagons because he expected them to hold. He placed Lethira’s rangers beyond his own scouts because he expected them to return. He ordered Falanaras near the front without assigning an orc to watch him.
No ceremony marked any of it.

The swamp thinned around them. Reeds gave way to dark soil, then to exposed red earth where little grew. The air dried. By evening, the eastern sky remained heavy with rain while the west held a bruised glow that did not belong to sunset.

They found the first refugee wagons at a broken milepost. Human families had abandoned them beside the road after cutting the traces. One wheel had melted into black glass. A child’s wooden horse lay under the axle, singed along one side. No bodies remained. Drag marks crossed the ditch toward the hills.
Mavren crouched beside the marks. “Felhounds. Four, perhaps five. Two carrying weight.”
An orc sergeant looked at the abandoned Alliance wagon. “Could have been bait.”
“Could have been children,” Tahu said.

Gorath sent scouts without asking which possibility mattered more. Lethira went with them. They returned after dark with blood on two arrows and three survivors: an old human teamster, a woman with a burned arm, and a boy who stared at the Horde soldiers as though rescue and capture had arrived wearing the same faces.

The woman recoiled when Althene Dawnward knelt beside her in black-and-crimson plate. Gold with a red heart gathered around the Blood Knight’s hands. M’uru’s pain entered Falanaras as Althene drew. The burned flesh cooled and began to close.
“What are you?” the woman whispered.
Althene kept working. “Available.”

They left the survivors at the next guarded post with a note for whichever Alliance patrol came searching. Gorath marked the road behind them as compromised. No council had negotiated the act. No herald proclaimed shared cause. Three living people remained alive because soldiers had encountered them before demons did.
The Legion had made cooperation simplest where politics had no time to name it.
The Blasted Lands began without a border.

Vegetation failed by degrees. Mud hardened into red plates. The last thorn bushes leaned east as if the country itself had tried to crawl away. Heat rose from fissures after sunset. Far ahead, green light pulsed against the low clouds and gave every ridge a second, sickly edge.

The road carried armies now. Horde supply trains moved west beneath escort and returned with wounded laid three across in wagons built for grain. Messengers passed at exhausted gallops. Demonic carcasses burned in trenches where warlocks and shamans argued over the safest way to destroy them. Twice the column halted for Alliance riders crossing a distant rise. Neither force approached the other. Both kept scouts between them.
On the third morning, wings darkened the south.
The demons flew too high for arrows at first, lean shapes circling above both roads. One peeled toward the Alliance column. Two descended upon the Horde wagons. Their hands kindled green.

Gorath’s axe struck earth. A ridge lifted beside the road and tilted over the nearest wagon as fel fire fell. Theron’s shield file locked beneath it. Red-gold radiance spread from shield to shield, strengthening the soldiers and teamsters within their reach. The first green impact broke across stone. The second struck the joined protection and drove every Blood Knight half a step into the road.

Lethira’s arrows rose with the Darkspear spears. Jazreth cast darkness above the lead demon’s face. It folded one wing to clear its sight. Tahu became a great hawk in a surge of feather and muscle, climbed through the creature’s turn, and tore the wing at its root.
The demon fell inside the column.

Falanaras met it with his sword already bright. He opened his pulse to the blade only far enough to deepen the radiance, accepted the answering cut beneath his ribs, and drove the edge through the demon’s burning chest. Mavren took its legs with his shield. Gorath’s next call brought stone around one claw before it reached a teamster.

The creature tried to form another spell. Falanaras felt the gathering fel current tighten behind its teeth. He drew a bounded measure from the unfinished working and released the stolen arcane charge in a blue-white burst. The demon’s invocation died in its throat. Lethira’s arrow entered through the open mouth.
It collapsed across the road, smoking.

The second demon climbed after Tahu. Far across the waste, gold flashed above the Alliance column. A compact stroke of holy force crossed the distance and struck the creature from below. Its flight broke. Tahu drove it down toward the Horde archers, who finished it before it could rise.
Falanaras looked east. A mounted human paladin lowered his hammer on the distant ridge. The face beneath the helm was too far away to know.
No salute passed between them. The Alliance column continued west. So did the Horde.
By afternoon, the Dark Portal rose above the horizon.

Distance made it appear smaller than memory. Each mile corrected the lie. The carved stone figures flanking the gateway grew until siege engines looked like toys at their feet. Green fire filled the opening from threshold to arch. Through it, another red world showed in fragments: broken ground, smoke, and fortifications burning beneath a sky that had forgotten blue.

The near-side approaches had become a battlefield built in layers. Old blood elf pylons lay split along the lower stairs. Horde earthworks held the north ridge. Alliance banners marked stone redoubts to the south. Between them, the Legion possessed the central descent often enough that neither army trusted a lull.
A horn sounded from the Horde works. Another answered from the Alliance side. Soldiers on both ridges rose behind shields as shapes moved within the green field.
Gorath did not hurry the column. “Close ranks. Rangers forward. Shield files around the wagons. If the Alliance fires, hold unless I answer. If the Legion comes, kill what reaches us.”
“Subtle policy,” Lethira said.
“I wrote it for elves,” Gorath replied.
The column laughed while tightening formation. A year earlier, the sound would have surprised them.
They waited below the north ridge until night.

The Legion tested the approaches twice. Felhounds came first, low and fast through the broken pylons. Horde archers killed most in the open ground. Alliance cannon took the flank of the pack that turned south. Later, armored demons descended the central stair behind shields burning green. Horde and Alliance artillery struck them from opposite ridges until the survivors withdrew through the gateway.
No truce flags flew. Each side watched the other between volleys. The common enemy had created an arrangement too necessary to admit and too fragile to name.

Near midnight, scouts returned from the far side with the route to a temporary Horde position marked in charcoal. One troll had lost an ear. A Farstrider carried burns from shoulder to hip and remained upright through anger alone. They reported broken Sunfury works, Legion emplacements along the ridges, and a narrow passage secured long enough for the next force to cross.
Gorath received the order before dawn. His column would move at first light, cross under covering fire, and reinforce the far-side position before the Legion closed the passage.

Falanaras slept for one hour against a supply crate. M’uru’s distant song entered his dreams and became the sound of the Portal’s fire. He woke with his hand closed around the hilt of a weapon Rynel had never seen him carry.
The company formed in the gray before sunrise.

Theron checked every shield strap in his file, then checked Falanaras’s breastplate seam without asking. Lethira distributed arrows and kept six black-fletched shafts separate from the rest. Jazreth drew a line of ash beneath each eye. Mavren tightened the angled grip around his imperfect wrist. Tahu pressed both palms to the barren ground and listened for whatever life or memory remained below it. Gorath walked the ranks with his axe on one shoulder.
They looked like a company because time had done the work uniforms could not.

The first time Falanaras had approached the Dark Portal, he had come beneath Kael’thas’s summons in a blood elf retinue that believed Outland contained an answer. Rynel’s death had placed him on that road. Liadrin had walked ahead of him without faith. Rommath and Astalor had carried plans whose full cost waited beyond the threshold. The prince’s name had made every hardship feel directed toward salvation.
That road had brought M’uru home in chains.

It had given Silvermoon relief, healers, soldiers, and an order strong enough to hold lines that would otherwise have broken. It had also taught Falanaras how easily necessity could make suffering useful. The power beneath his breastbone proved both truths each time he drew breath.

Kael’thas no longer waited beyond the gateway as prince, promise, or destination. Somewhere in the broken world ahead, his forces served a cause Silvermoon had disowned. Outland had ceased to be the future offered to the sin’dorei. It had become another front that could send enemies through their door.

Falanaras looked south across the divided battlefield. Alliance soldiers formed beneath blue standards. Paladins moved among them with gold held close to their armor. He could not see Edric. He could not see Caelir. The distance did not lessen what Hillsbrad had left between them.
Nearly a year had given the spared life time to become anything. Falanaras did not know what Edric had made of it. Mercy had preserved the question. It had never promised him the answer.

Behind him, the Horde column waited: orcs beneath red banners, trolls with spears and shadow charms, tauren carrying staves and heavy packs, Forsaken standing too still among the living, and blood elves in crimson-edged plate. Some still distrusted the green in sin’dorei eyes. Some still heard the wrongness in Blood Knight radiance. They had nevertheless placed their wounded beneath Theron’s shields and their flanks beneath Lethira’s arrows. They had given Falanaras command over their lives and taken command over his.
Belonging remained larger than what they possessed.
They had reached trust in the places where trust mattered first.
Gorath stopped beside him at the foot of the stairs. “You have crossed this before.”
“Yes.”
“Anything useful to say?”
Falanaras watched green fire move across the vast opening. “The first step feels longer than it is.”
Gorath grunted. “That is not useful.”
“It is all the Portal taught me.”
The signal horn sounded above them.

Horde artillery opened from the north ridge. Alliance cannon answered from the south. Their shots crossed above the central stair and struck demonic positions visible through the gateway. Green fire buckled. For several breaths, the way into Outland stood open beneath impacts from enemies who had agreed on nothing except the target.
Gorath raised his axe. “Forward.”
The company climbed.

Theron’s shields surrounded the front ranks. Lethira’s rangers moved between files with arrows ready. Jazreth’s darkness gathered close enough to receive whatever waited beyond sight. Mavren marched with his repaired arm fixed around the angled grip. Tahu’s staff struck each stair with the steadiness of a second heartbeat. Gorath’s carved stones clicked beneath the Horde pennants at his belt.
The phoenix standard rose among them.

At the threshold, M’uru’s pain sharpened through Falanaras’s bond. Rynel’s last command returned with it. Kael’thas’s severed promise followed. So did his father beneath the ruins of House Dawnspear, Liadrin’s broken prayers at the inner gate, Edric kneeling beneath his sword, and Caelir turning away across a battlefield.
He carried every cost. None became lighter because another war required him.
Falanaras stepped into the green fire.
The first step was no longer than the rest.
